newsitem.title: CHINA: China stock markets plunge as Hong Kong party ends.
newsitem.headline: China stock markets plunge as Hong Kong party ends.

text.p: China's stock markets plunged on Monday after investors fled the market and declared the Hong Kong handover party well and truly over, brokers said.

The return of the British colony of Hong Kong to Chinese rule had boosted sentiment for months. But since passage of the historic event on July 1 investors have awoken to reality and found uncertainty and negative news on the horizon, they said.
"People now aren't sure what the return of Hong Kong means to the securities markets," said a broker at a foreign securities firm in Shanghai. "They're holding back from buying."
Shanghai's foreign currency B index closed down 2.080 points or 2.73 percent to 74.145 points on turnover of $5.672 million.
Shenzhen's hard currency B share index plunged 7.71 points or 5.7 percent to end at 127.69 on turnover of HK$50 million.

China's market regulators on Friday reaffirmed their goal of purging the B share market -- technically reserved for foreigners -- of domestic investors, hurting sentiment when trading resumed on Monday.
But the domestic currency A share indices took a heavier beating, pushed down by persistent rumours about further government moves aimed at keeping the markets stable.
The Shanghai A index ended down 66.196 points or 5.46 percent at 1,145.251 on turnover of 4.098 billion yuan.
Shenzhen's A share index dived 33.28 points or 8.08 percent to 378.35 on turnover of 4.8 billion yuan.

"The correction in the A shares is normal given the sharp rises before the handover," said an analyst at an Asian securities firm in Shanghai. "But investors are scared and they're liquidating their positions."
In addition, a flood of expected listings on both the A and B markets has damaged sentiment as investors turn away from existing shares to wait for the new issues, brokers said.

With the Hong Kong handover now a thing of the past and the eyes of the world turned elsewhere, domestic investors feel Beijing is more likely to announce harsh measures to cool the markets, they said.
"Rumours of tighter curbs on speculation, which have circulated in the markets before, were heard again, triggering some panic selling," said one broker.
Persistent rumours that the government would take steps to list some types of non-traded shares or would act to prevent state enterprises speculating in shares have plagued the market in recent days.

Shenzhen investors have also run for cover on speculation the exchange would boost the transaction settlement period to three days for A and B shares, from the one-day settlement for A shares and immediate settlement for B shares.
The combination of concrete events, such as new share issues, with rumours of further government measures would continue to send the markets lower in the short term, brokers said.

Investors were looking toward interim results, the bulk of which will be reported in August, before returning to buy selected shares of companies that showed strong performances in the first half of 1997, they said.
The 15th Communist Party congress, which is expected later this year, would be a bellwether event for foreign investors waiting to see the roadmap for China's future development, brokers said.
